name: David Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a front-end loader at a big bauxite mine, the red dirt they make aluminium from. Mostly I'm at the stockpile by the crusher, feeding ore into the hopper at the right pace so it doesn't choke, and cleaning up spillage around the conveyors. I'm a year and a half in and still learning to keep an even feed; the crusher operator, Pete, gets on the radio when I overload it. The best bit is the smoko at ten, when the whole crew sits in the crib hut and argues about football.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Sara, she's a primary school teacher, and we're getting married next spring in her parents' church. We rent for now but I've got about eight months saved, and my dad and I own a small block of units together that brings in rent. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly Sara makes me use it for wedding lists. There are two other bauxite mines and an alumina refinery within an hour, so there's work around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fine by me. Steady is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was overblown, and that good honest work doesn't change much. At the crib hut I'd say the computer blokes got carried away. I don't post anything online, Sara does all that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I can plan the wedding and a family without second-guessing. The mine's busy, and loader drivers are always needed. My biggest worry is the bauxite price and whether the refinery keeps running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get married in the spring, keep working, and buy a house within two years. I'd ask to do the haul truck ticket so I can earn more on overtime. I'd keep saving the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend on first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding, then a house deposit. Sara wants a yard for kids, and I'd like that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any pressure already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the refinery had a scare last year with power costs. When the alumina refinery nearly shut over power prices last year, I learned my job depends on things nobody at the mine controls.

At the crib hut I'd say the **computer blokes** got carried away.
think: He can plan the **wedding and a family** without second-guessing.
His worry is the **bauxite price** and whether the refinery keeps running.
do: Get **married in the spring** at Sara's parents' church.
Buy a **house within two years**, with a yard for kids.
Do the **haul truck ticket** to earn more overtime.

fieldNote: His **family plans** are the centre of every answer.

steps.text: Marry Sara in the spring at her parents' church
Buy a house with a yard within two years
Get the haul truck ticket for overtime shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds more real. Some of that's already starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that we should get proper apprenticeships and training out of it, not just new machines. At church I'd say families need to stick together through changes. I wouldn't go online about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my loader job is safe for a while, because robots are slow to spread here. But the planning and the scheduling would go to software. That means fewer supervisors and more pressure on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get married, but I'd hold off on the house for a year. I'd ask about an apprenticeship in the workshop, because that's a real trade. I'd try the new tools once the others had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sara about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're fine, but I want a trade behind me. Before Sara (my fiancée) and I have kids, I want a real trade behind me, not just a loader ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sara's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching's safe, I think. Kids need a person. So she's the steady one.

steps.text: Put the house purchase off by one year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before we'd even have kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government should make companies keep people on and train them. At church I'd say we look after each other. I'd vote for anyone promising apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my loader job goes by 2031. Feeding a crusher is simple for a robot. Feeding the crusher at the bauxite mine is simple enough that a robot could do my job by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still marry Sara but hold off on kids and a house. I'd start the workshop apprenticeship right away and work all the overtime I could. I'd keep the rental units as our safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd want to protect Sara and our plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to. But Sara's family is here, and her teaching job too. I'd try to stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we need to hold on to the units, whatever happens. That rent might be what keeps us going.

I'd vote for anyone promising **apprenticeships**, and say we look after each other.

He's **junior** at the crusher, and the job is simple enough to hand over.
do: Still marry Sara but **delay kids** and the house.

feel: **Anxious**, wanting to protect Sara and their plans.
S2.quote: Feeding the crusher at the bauxite mine is simple enough that a robot could do my job by 2031.
fieldNote: He'd change **family plans** before anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots about eight. More time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it right, and companies should run proper apprenticeships. I'd say it at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I can get a trade before 2034. Five years is long enough for me to finish a fitter's apprenticeship before the robots start feeding the crusher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start the apprenticeship in the first year. Get married, buy a smaller house. Keep the rental units and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel more in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still have kids on the same timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a year or two later. I'd want the trade finished first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots can fix robots, the trade might not last. But it's a better bet than a loader.

I'd say so at work and at **church**, where people would agree.

S3.quote: Five years is long enough for me to finish a fitter's apprenticeship before the robots start feeding the crusher.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **finish a trade** before robots arrive.

He sees a trade as a **better bet**, not a guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a good amount of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to train up and get ready, and it's on the companies and families to plan. I'd say it at the crib hut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think it's fine for me. Ten years of warning means I can marry Sara, buy the house and still finish a trade before any robot drives my loader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get married, buy the house, start a trade in a couple of years. Keep the rental units with my dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit uneasy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have kids on schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Ten years is enough time to be sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not knowing which trades will last. And the older guys at the mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits right when Sara and I are starting out. What would help is real apprenticeships, paid, with companies keeping workers on while they train. Pay me to learn a trade while I'm still driving the loader, and I'll stay loyal to the bauxite mine for life.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the wedding. Big life plans are what this affects most for people my age.

headlineQuote: Pay me to learn a trade while I'm still driving the loader, and I'll stay loyal to the bauxite mine for life.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old** loader driver at a bauxite mine, feeding the crusher.
He's engaged to Sara, a teacher, and has **eight months saved** plus rental units with his dad.
He takes up tools **once proven** and uses AI now and then.
His answers centre on **family plans** and getting a real trade.
He's **calm** in the plateau and **anxious** in the faster AGI pictures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits just as he and Sara are starting out.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships**, with companies keeping workers on while they train.
